summary:
ARES-NAV is an offline, voice-guided augmented reality (AR) navigation and safety assistant designed for crewed surface exploration in Mars’ Gale Crater. By fusing four distinct NASA datasets—optical/topographic imagery (HiRISE), radiation (RAD), thermal/atmospheric metrics (REMS), and spectral data (CRISM)—into a synchronized mission-control map and helmet HUD, ARES-NAV enables astronauts to navigate harsh Martian terrain without real-time support from Earth.
Exploring Mars involves a 20+ minute communication delay, steep slopes, high radiation, thick spacesuit gloves that hinder screen interaction, and sudden dust storms that reduce visibility to zero. ARES-NAV solves these challenges through automated hazard-avoidance routing, a strict 50-meter line-of-sight buddy protocol between Science and Safety specialists, and hands-free AR rock scanning.
Most importantly, when blinding dust storms or radiation spikes occur, ARES-NAV prioritizes crew survival by guiding astronauts to Habitat Alpha or natural crater shielding using continuous English voice navigation, ground AR arrows, and directional glove vibrations.
details:
How It Works & Key Features

ARES-NAV operates as an offline, dual-view navigation and safety system inside a calibrated 500m x 500m sector of Mars’ Gale Crater. It synchronizes a Top-Down Mission Control Map with a First-Person Astronaut Helmet HUD. Explorers operate in pairs—a Science Specialist (A1) and a Safety Specialist (A2)—linked by a real-time 50-meter line-of-sight rule. Users can select geological targets (such as ancient groundwater boxwork formations), view live distance and spacesuit pace countdowns (~0.6 m/s), and perform hands-free AR spectral scans. When environmental hazards occur—such as steep slopes (>15%), thermal drops (-82°C in shadow), high radiation spikes (>1.50 mSv/hr), or blinding dust storms—ARES-NAV automatically calculates escape paths to Habitat Alpha or Natural Terrain Shielding (crater shadows).

Benefits & Intended Impact

Because Earth is over 20 minutes away by radio, Martian astronauts must rely on autonomous local tools. ARES-NAV reduces cognitive load, saves critical oxygen and EVA time by identifying high-value targets immediately, and prevents crew separation. Its intended impact extends beyond Mars: the system is ready for testing in Earth-based Mars analog stations (such as MDRS) and can be adapted for NASA’s Artemis lunar surface missions, where astronauts face similar extreme lighting, terrain,and communication challenges.

Creativity & Human-Centered Design Factors

Instead of simply drawing lines on a map, our team focused on human factors and zero-visibility survival. We considered that pressurized spacesuit gloves make touching screens difficult and Martian dust storms can blind a helmet visor completely. To solve this, ARES-NAV combines 3-sense emergency guidance: glowing ground AR chevrons, directional gauntlet vibrations (haptic alerts), and a smart, non-overlapping English voice assistant (SpeechSynthesis) that gives real-time distance updates every 30 meters. We also strictly separated verified NASA measurements from simulated target values to ensure scientific integrity.

Tools, Software & AI Transparency

To build and deploy this interactive web prototype rapidly, we utilized modern web technologies (React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Web Audio API, and Browser SpeechSynthesis API) alongside Lovable, an AI-assisted web development platform. While AI tools accelerated front-end coding and deployment, all scientific research, NASA dataset integration (Mars Trek, MRO HiRISE, Curiosity RAD & REMS), safety protocols, and user-experience logic were conceptualized, verified, and structured by our team.
